knowledge_type_note: A strategic method: it prescribes a way of playing — reduce what the opponent can do — rather than naming a board feature.

attributions.note: The formula and the surrounding theory are his, and the maxim was verified verbatim in the primary text.

history.notes: Verified in the full text of My System, where the formula appears twice, once as the motto of an illustrative game.

engine_era_note: Engines play restraining moves constantly, and human commentary reaches for this vocabulary to explain them. The concept is unrevised.

preconditions: A move that reduces the opponent's options rather than advancing one's own plan
indicators_for: An enemy pawn break is prevented or made costly
An enemy piece is denied its best square before it gets there
The opponent's pawn mass is fixed and can no longer expand
indicators_against: The advance being restrained was not something the opponent wanted anyway
false_positive_traps: Restraint is not the same as passivity. It reduces the opponent's options; a passive move merely fails to increase yours.
Like prophylaxis, it is easy to assert after the fact about any quiet move. Name the advance being prevented.

typical_plans: Fix the enemy pawn mass before attacking it
Deny the square an enemy piece needs
Restrain, blockade, destroy — in that order
strategic_consequences: Reduces the opponent to waiting, which is often decisive by itself

exceptions: Restraining an advance the opponent did not want is a wasted move.
In sharp positions speed beats restraint.
limitations: Not detectable from a static position: it is defined by what a move prevents.

MEASURED 2026-09-02, against the record's own second trap: 'like prophylaxis, it is easy to assert after the fact about any quiet move. Name the advance being prevented.' This base does NOT name the advance. Its matcher measures the change in the opponent's SAFE destination squares across the move, which is a count and not a name, and reports the count. Naming the prevented advance needs a model of what the opponent intended, which nothing here has. The count is the honest half and it is what is reported; the record's instruction is not met and is recorded here rather than looking unnoticed.
misconceptions: That restraint is defensive. Nimzowitsch treats it as the first stage of an attacking plan.
That it is the same as the blockade. The blockade is restraint made permanent by a piece.

examples.note: Black's e6 pawn cannot advance and the whole position is built to keep it that way — Nimzowitsch's note four moves earlier reads 'The immobility of the e-pawn is now greater than ever.' Restraint rather than prophylaxis: nothing specific is being prevented, the opponent's general mobility is being reduced, which is the distinction this record exists to preserve. FEN verified by replay.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-quiet-move-that-restrains-nothing`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Kd1 in a fully locked position is a quiet, non-committal move that does not lose anything. Quiet moves in blocked positions are the shape prophylaxis and restraint are usually claimed about. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's traps, both of them: "Restraint is not the same as passivity. It reduces the opponent's options; a passive move merely fails to increase yours." And: "Like prophylaxis, it is easy to assert after the fact about any quiet move. Name the advance being prevented." No advance is being prevented — the structure prevents them all by itself, and it did so before the move. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API is silent on restraint. The matcher asks whether the move reduces the opponent's safe destinations rather than whether it is quiet, which is the first trap built rather than quoted; and it is move-based, so it cannot be asserted after the fact about the position. This is the case that a keyword rule would fail: every word in the record about quiet moves in blocked positions is present here and the concept is absent.

This is the negative half: the position is fully locked, nothing is being restrained because nothing can advance in the first place, and the evaluation confirms that no advantage attaches to the quiet move that was played.

by_level.beginner: Stop their pawns from moving forward before you try to win them.
by_level.intermediate: Restraint: reduce what they can do. It is the first step of restrain, blockade, destroy — stop the pawn, then block it, then take it.
by_level.advanced: The general case of the blockade. Distinguish it from prophylaxis: prophylaxis prevents a specific idea, restraint reduces general mobility.
by_level.master: Nimzowitsch's Hemmungstheorie. The cost is the same as prophylaxis's — the move does nothing for you, so what it prevents must be worth preventing.

by_depth.short: Stop them expanding before you attack.
by_depth.normal: Restraint: preventing enemy pawns and pieces from advancing, as progress in its own right. It is the first stage of Nimzowitsch's formula — first restrain, then blockade, finally destroy.
by_depth.deep: The idea that reducing the opponent's options counts as progress even when it improves nothing of yours. The formula is in My System verbatim, and the ORDER is its content: a pawn is stopped from advancing, then physically blocked, and only then attacked. Restraint is the general case and the blockade the concrete one. It sits close to prophylaxis, and the distinction worth keeping is that prophylaxis prevents a specific idea while restraint reduces general mobility — Nimzowitsch's own term for the wider strategy was Hemmungstheorie, inhibition strategy.

explanations.lesson: Before attacking something, stop it moving. A pawn you have fixed is a pawn you can attack at leisure.

definition_short: Stopping enemy pawns and pieces from advancing before doing anything else. The first stage of Nimzowitsch's formula: first restrain, then blockade, finally destroy.
definition_long:
Restraint is the idea that preventing your opponent's expansion counts as PROGRESS, even though it improves nothing of yours. Nimzowitsch's formula appears verbatim in My System: 'First restrain, then blockade and finally destroy!' — and the order is the content. A pawn is first stopped from advancing, then physically blocked, and only then attacked.

It is the general case of which the blockade is the concrete one. Restraint may be exercised by control of a square, by pressure that makes an advance costly, or by fixing a pawn so that moving it loses something. The blockade is restraint made permanent by putting a piece in the way.

The idea is close to prophylaxis and the two are often conflated. The useful distinction: prophylaxis prevents a specific IDEA the opponent has, while restraint reduces their general MOBILITY. Nimzowitsch's own term for the broader strategy was Hemmungstheorie, usually rendered as inhibition strategy.

Its cost is the same as prophylaxis's: a restraining move often does nothing for you, so it is only worth the tempo if what it prevents was worth preventing.
